Eskom Alternatives

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Your Eskom load-shedding survival plan

Summary:
Eskom is struggling to keep the lights on. The inconvenience is staggering. This is the essential survival guide. See what you can harness in your immediate environment to get through the four-hour stretches of load shedding that will become ever more frequent. And we help you process the change and financial shock.

Further information:
We explore over-the-counter and do-it-yourself alternatives for generating enough power to stay online, productive, connected. These alternatives won't take you off the grid completely, but they will keep the lights and laptops on. But if you don't choose well, you run the risk of spending far more than you should. Cheap solutions may not be the best.

Builders' Warehouse's DIY guru will put together packages that will serve large and small households (they've agreed to participate without being branded).

An alternative energy engineer (consultant from Blacklight) will explain how to size a solution for a given home or office.

The Naked Scientist will explain the basic principles of how a home is put together and how to get alternatives to kick in - he will also look forward to solutions we may look forward to in the near future as our reliance on coal-powered energy comes to a reluctant end.

We also call on a financial shrink to help process the transition and shock of dealing with an end to hopes that the problem will be solved quickly and how to deal with the unforeseen expense.

The options we will unpack include solar, which is expensive and has a short lifespan, but can take you off the grid in time, if you plan it well. We'll analyse the benefits of a UPS, car battery with inverter, explaining the need for inverters. We will weigh the options of generators and gas and look forward to new technologies that may in time prove more fruitful - including hydro (water milll power generation), biogas, biomas, waste and fuel cells.

Press Release:


Load-shedding proof
How far will R15000 go towards making the average South African home load-shedding proof? Carte Blanche explores cost-effective alternatives to electricity for a home that can least afford to be without power – a small-scale shelter for abandoned babies.





Script:


SCRIPT_ESKOM ALTERNATIVES

VO: What are the best load shedding solutions available for an average family home on a modest budget? To find out, we put up R15 000 to implement simple alternatives available from neighbourhood stores. The McQueens of Benoni not only work from home but home-school two of their four kids and last year, they also opened one of their rooms to abandoned and abused babies. Carte Blanche worked with Charmaine and Kent to see what they needed and what was available to keep them going during a blackout.
CHARMAINE MCQUEEN: it came as quite a shock for me to receive babies in the state that I’ve received them…I don’t think you can ever be prepared…we’ve had a baby eaten by rats…and heart-breaking stories.
VO: The Swallows Nest Baby Shelter runs as a green home – meaning they use no chemicals and they work to keep it pollution-free.
CHARMAINE MCQUEEN: The babies come to us malnourished, which affect their guts quite adversely – so any form of absorption of chemicals affects them quite adversely – they break out in eczema asthma, various kind of allergic reactions.
ISABEL DUBE: We ladies sit together, we talk about the babies, and work out how to go the extra mile – it’s not a job, it’s a calling – with this calling it is very it’s very hard to see them go.
VO: Once nurtured back to health, the shelter aims to have the babies adopted. Already lacking in development, their progress is a race against time. The McQueens cannot afford to be without power, but they also have to find ways to limit their use of expensive electricity.
KENT MCQUEEN: Big impact on our home, there’s impact of space, there’s impact of living together, on your children, and it’s all good been good, but obviously it’s resource-heavy if you wanna call it that. We’ve obviously seen the electricity bills go up because you’re bathing and preparing for babies, for care givers. Food has gone up. All sorts of things have increased, drastically actually.
VO: Much like any suburban home or small home office, the McQueens need an affordable, accessible solution for staying functional when the grid goes down.
CHARMAINE MCQUEEN: It really challenges us because we have to ensure that we have sufficient warm water, boiled warm water for baby bottles and we are not just making a few bottles a day – we are making many many bottles a day. It is also just preparing bath time. Bath time is a wonderful time of the day, because it relaxes the babies and they go to bed soon after. So when we don’t have hot water to bath babies, it’ smakes it difficult putting them down, they get a little bit disturbed because their routine are not quite the same – but if it’s disrupted, babies don’t go down so easily. It’s difficult to work with the babies by candle light…it just makes things complicated for us.
VO: We first looked at DO-IT-YOURSELF SOLUTIONS with Andrew Donkin, who engages daily with consumers on social media.
ANDREW DONKIN: There’s a number of different solutions we can look at – we can look at generators to get your power up and running straight away…
BONITA NUTTALL: Just take me somewhere, start me somewhere, I’ll follow you.
ANDREW DONKIN: We’ve got an entry-level…1000 KVA, 1000 watts – that’s enough to start your light globes, your TV, computer and the smaller little appliances like that. You then got slightly larger one, medium size 5,5KVA – basically 55000watts. Now you can start putting on your hair dryer, geyser – your geyser would use 3-4000 watts…so a geyser alone would use most of that power, so keep that in mind.
BONITA NUTTALL: If I bought any of these three here, where would I place them in my home?
ANDREW DONKIN: It’s important to have it in a well-ventilated area, not in the main home, you don’t want all the fumes going into your house – you want those fumes to waft away into the atmosphere, and where it’s safe. Also the noise too, there’s nothing worse than a big open empty garage, because it just acts like an amplifier in a cathedral, it’s gonna amplify that sound.
VO: Donkin explained that to get the right generator, we had to study the labels on appliances that show the number of watts they use to start up and run. Combined, this would be the size of the power solution we would need. But if we wanted to run the generator through the electrical distribution board it would no longer be considered DO-IT-YOURSELF. We’d need a qualified electrician if we didn’t want to destroy the house and generator in the process.
BONITA NUTTALL: Very crucial question here…how much do these generators it cost?
ANDREW DONKIN: They start off at R1800and you’re working your way up…you can go up to 35, 60, 70-thousand rand.
VO: All the experts we consulted agreed that the first step to becoming more electricity savvy is to replace appliances that waste energy. MEASURE how much power each appliance uses and unplug what’s unnecessary. COVER geysers to RETAIN heat. REPLACE old-style light bulbs that use twelve times more energy and THAT over time cost a lot more than LED bulbs. Replace old-style HOLLOW shower heads with a head that has a small regulator that lets through half the amount of water for the same effect. This will ensure the geyser uses less energy to fill up again.
ANDREW DONKIN: You’ve got the induction cooker, which use a lot less power as well.
VO: The McQueen household had already put some electricity saving measures in place.
KENT MCQUEEN: Makes a big difference to put in geyser timer…and also take big users of electricity to gas or potentially solar.
VO: Solar panels may be durable, clean and quiet…but adding enough panels and batteries to generate and store power gets very expensive very quickly.
ANDREW DONKIN: We’ve got a solar panel, that’s gonna go up on the roof, then basically you’re going to connect that down to your regulator…from there into your battery…from the battery you can use the DC or you can take it to an inverter where you can convert it to AC.
BONITA NUTTALL: So Andrew tell us costs, what are we looking at?
ANDREW DONKIN: A 50-watt panel is around about R2000, you’ve got the 220-watt panel that’s about R5,500 – you’ve got your batteries which is about R2000, you’ve got the regulators which is about R800…and you’ve got your inverter which is about R3000…so to get set up with the basic kit – just on the components, you’re looking at R8000.
BONITA NUTTALL: Fantastic – so we can burn four light bulbs?
ANDREW DONKIN: No you can burn a bit more with that, but yes, it’s the basic entry level – all you need to do then is start increasing your battery sizes and your panels as well.
VO: For the Swallows Nest Baby Shelter a generator that could wake babies, emit fumes or run out of diesel wasn’t an option…solar panels and batteries could work, but the number of panels needed exceeded the budget. Carte Blanche asked Builders Warehouse to devise the best complete solution for R15,000. Their supplier Ellies recommended the latest uninterrupted power supply and battery that charges itself when the power is on. Adrian Nel said the UPS could run for hours, depending how many appliances were plugged in.
ADRIAN NEL: The UPS system is a silent system – it’s running at this stage, we don’t hear it and the minute the lights kick off the UPS kicks in within milliseconds, you don’t even know that the lights have tripped. For example on this system if we drew 400 watts, it would allow us to have 9 hours running time just on this unit. But if it’s flat, been drawn all the way down, it will take 6-8 hours to get it up again…
VO: Again, installing the UPS into the DB board and isolating some parts to stay on the UPS has to be done by a qualified electrician.
ADRIAN NEL: So we’ve taken the washing machines and fridges off. In this situation they wanna have lights to see what they do with the children and a couple of plugs just to have a backup in case they need small items like humidifier. But with the load shedding they’re gonna have, they’re gonna be self-sufficient. And that’s what most of the consumers wanna do – they just wanna get through the load shedding -- a lot of guys it’s the alarm system that you wanna keep running. We’ve done a light that works purely on solar – it’s a floodlight with a sensor. So there’s a lot of different items you can use just to get through the load shedding period.
VO: So R15,000 can buy a UPS and battery system; 10 dimmable LED bulbs that give a soft light that won’t wake babies at night; a geyser timer and a solar security light. Electricians’ fees fell outside the budget. In the process of advising us, Builders Warehouse’s Steven Botha became so inspired by the work done at the shelter, that he motivated for his company to match Carte Blanche’s donation. They rebuilt some run-down outbuildings so that the shelter could run independently from the main house.
STEVEN BOTHA: For me it was just about space, brightness safety…getting them to be in a home and not just squashed in a little room…and the second thing was how to make it load-shedding proof for these children.
VO: The shelter now has its own blackout-proof home – just on the other side of the garden, which makes it much easier for the McQueens to care for the babies.
ISABEL DUBE: We say hallelujah…I’m so happy what is happening – this system is going to take us through. . we are going to have a better house, a better Swallows Nest.

ANDREW DONKIN: A 50-watt panel is around about R2000, you’ve got the 220-watt panel that’s about R5,500 – you’ve got your batteries which is about R2000, you’ve got the regulators which is about R800…and you’ve got your inverter which is about R3000…so to get set up with the basic kit – just on the components, you’re looking at R8000. BONITA NUTTALL: Fantastic – so we can burn four light bulbs? ANDREW DONKIN: No you can burn a bit more with that, but yes, it’s the basic entry level – all you need to do then is start increasing your battery sizes and your panels as well. VO: For the Swallows Nest Baby Shelter a generator that could wake babies, emit fumes or run out of diesel wasn’t an option…solar panels and batteries could work, but the number of panels needed exceeded the budget. Carte Blanche asked Builders Warehouse to devise the best complete solution for R15,000. Their supplier Ellies recommended the latest uninterrupted power supply and battery that charges itself when the power is on. Adrian Nel said the UPS could run for hours, depending how many appliances were plugged in. ADRIAN NEL: The UPS system is a silent system – it’s running at this stage, we don’t hear it and the minute the lights kick off the UPS kicks in within milliseconds, you don’t even know that the lights have tripped. For example on this system if we drew 400 watts, it would allow us to have 9 hours running time just on this unit. But if it’s flat, been drawn all the way down, it will take 6-8 hours to get it up again… VO: Again, installing the UPS into the DB board and isolating some parts to stay on the UPS has to be done by a qualified electrician. ADRIAN NEL: So we’ve taken the washing machines and fridges off. In this situation they wanna have lights to see what they do with the children and a couple of plugs just to have a backup in case they need small items like humidifier. But with the load shedding they’re gonna have, they’re gonna be self-sufficient. And that’s what most of the consumers wanna do – they just wanna get through the load shedding -- a lot of guys it’s the alarm system that you wanna keep running. We’ve done a light that works purely on solar – it’s a floodlight with a sensor. So there’s a lot of different items you can use just to get through the load shedding period. VO: So R15,000 can buy a UPS and battery system; 10 dimmable LED bulbs that give a soft light that won’t wake babies at night; a geyser timer and a solar security light. Electricians’ fees fell outside the budget. In the process of advising us, Builders Warehouse’s Steven Botha became so inspired by the work done at the shelter, that he motivated for his company to match Carte Blanche’s donation. They rebuilt some run-down outbuildings so that the shelter could run independently from the main house. STEVEN BOTHA: For me it was just about space, brightness safety…getting them to be in a home and not just squashed in a little room…and the second thing was how to make it load-shedding proof for these children. VO: The shelter now has its own blackout-proof home – just on the other side of the garden, which makes it much easier for the McQueens to care for the babies. ISABEL DUBE: We say hallelujah…I’m so happy what is happening – this system is going to take us through. . we are going to have a better house, a better Swallows Nest.

metadata.Summary: Eskom is struggling to keep the lights on. The inconvenience is staggering. This is the essential survival guide. See what you can harness in your immediate environment to get through the four-hour stretches of load shedding that will become ever more frequent. And we help you process the change and financial shock.
metadata.Further information: We explore over-the-counter and do-it-yourself alternatives for generating enough power to stay online, productive, connected. These alternatives won't take you off the grid completely, but they will keep the lights and laptops on. But if you don't choose well, you run the risk of spending far more than you should. Cheap solutions may not be the best. Builders' Warehouse's DIY guru will put together packages that will serve large and small households (they've agreed to participate without being branded). An alternative energy engineer (consultant from Blacklight) will explain how to size a solution for a given home or office. The Naked Scientist will explain the basic principles of how a home is put together and how to get alternatives to kick in - he will also look forward to solutions we may look forward to in the near future as our reliance on coal-powered energy comes to a reluctant end. We also call on a financial shrink to help process the transition and shock of dealing with an end to hopes that the problem will be solved quickly and how to deal with the unforeseen expense. The options we will unpack include solar, which is expensive and has a short lifespan, but can take you off the grid in time, if you plan it well. We'll analyse the benefits of a UPS, car battery with inverter, explaining the need for inverters. We will weigh the options of generators and gas and look forward to new technologies that may in time prove more fruitful - including hydro (water milll power generation), biogas, biomas, waste and fuel cells.
